Mythbusters is entertainment science, which is to say it's not really all that descriptive of what scientists actually do. Their testing is usually far from rigorous, and on occasion outright broken. Not to say they get everything wrong, but it's hard to know when it is wrong since they don't really publish retractions. What the show is good at, is getting kids more interested in science. So I suppose taking the good with the bad we're probably still left with a net positive.

Goodbye Mythbusters. You weren't perfect, but you made it fun.

You said it well. Mythbusters should never be conflated with actual scientific testing because they often choose flawed testing methods. As a result, their conclusions will show the bias introduced by the flawed apparatus or measurement methods. While they did not rigorously do scientific testing, they did at least apply clever thoughts that nonscientific people could relate to and be inspired by. I have always been of mixed opinion whether this show was a good example for getting kids into science because of these flaws. Most kids would turn away from a show that included the actual rigor of science, but using flawed and entertaining methods of testing myths does not truly give a taste of real science. I always fear we will raise kids with the expectation that science is always crazy, chaotic and fun. The popular culture of science perpetuates this at every opportunity. We have good intentions, but like Mythbusters, our methods are flawed.

I think this show does more to inspire the self-proclaimed garage inventor kid than it does future physicists, chemists and the like. Hopefully as the kids raised on Mythbusters age they will gain a true knowledge and understanding that science is thorough, difficult, not glamorous and often boring. The true scientists will be the ones who continue on unabated after learning these things. The rest will at least be able to have moderately educated discussions that are based on some thought rather than pure blissful ignorance, or at least I hope so.

I'm often reminded of the person who wants to learn guitar, but feels that it must be some innate skill that a good player possesses to allow him to play well when really it's a great deal of practice and attention to detail. We all know the guy who learns one or two songs and never goes any further, but he at least has a slightly better understanding of it than the person who never tries.

Yes the show is a misrepresentation, but at least it is an indication that science does not have to be 100% boring - and worse - seemingly pointless all the time. That there can be a gratifying payoff even if you're not the next Einstein. Even if the show only succeeds in educating the layman to not be quite as lay, I'd call that a win.
